title: Ganesh Chaturthi: the guest who wants love
hookLine: Ganesha comes home as a guest, and a handful of rice beats a feast
carry: god accepts what's offered with love
tomorrow: who is the Goddess the gods couldn't win without?

cards: In cities across Maharashtra, in late summer, you'll see something like a parade and a house move at once.

A family walks down the street with drums and cymbals, and in the middle, carried in someone's arms or in a car with the windows down, is a clay Ganesha, garlanded, sometimes taller than the person carrying him.
He's coming to stay: for a day and a half, or five days, or ten. And when he leaves, he'll be carried to the water.

teach.b: Chaturthi means the fourth: the fourth day of the bright half of the month of Bhadrapada, usually in August or September. It's kept as Ganesha's birthday. For these days he is treated exactly like an honored guest.
In a rite called pranapratishtha, establishing the breath of life, the family invites him into the clay image.
Then he's welcomed the way you'd welcome family off a long trip: a seat, water, flowers, red hibiscus and durva grass, modaks, songs morning and evening. That's not only a festival custom.

teach.h: PUJA: GOD RECEIVED AS A GUEST.
teach.b: It's how Hindu worship, puja, is built: God received as a guest. And a story families love to tell, told many ways and not from the oldest texts, says what this guest really wants.
Kubera, the god of wealth, throws a grand feast to show off his riches, and Ganesha comes as the guest. Ganesha eats. And eats.
The kitchens empty, and he's still hungry, until Kubera runs, embarrassed, to Shiva.

teach.h: A HANDFUL OF RICE, GIVEN HUMBLY.
teach.b: Kubera is given one handful of roasted rice and told to offer it humbly. He does, and Ganesha is full at last.
In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna teaches the same thing in plain words: a leaf, a flower, a fruit, a little water, offered with love, I accept.
So a family with a small clay Ganesha and one plate of modaks hasn't done less than the giant public pandals that grew from Pune in the 1890s.
On the last day the guest is thanked and carried to the water: visarjan, letting go. The love was the offering all along.

how: Families bring a clay Ganesha home on Ganesh Chaturthi, install and worship it for one and a half to ten days with flowers, durva grass, modaks and aarti, then carry it in procession to water for immersion; many cities also hold large public pandals.

o: Ganesha's fourth day, when a clay guest is welcomed home
the night of the Goddess's win over a buffalo demon
the day brothers have threads tied on their wrists

p: inviting the god into the image
worship built like welcoming a guest
a feast that couldn't fill Ganesha

s: a bigger offering pleases Ganesha more
in the Kubera story a feast fails, and a handful of rice given humbly fills him.
puja is built like welcoming an honored guest
a seat, water, flowers, food, songs, then a fond farewell.
in the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says the love behind an offering is what he accepts
a leaf, a flower, a fruit, a little water, offered with devotion (Gita 9.26).

games.q: your family's clay Ganesha is small this year, with one plate of modaks. a cousin posts a giant pandal and calls yours 'cute'. by today's teaching, what fits?
o: a handful offered with love is enough; that's what Ganesha wants.
go bigger next year so Ganesha notices you.
skip it; small pujas don't really count.
games.why: Kubera's feast couldn't fill him; a handful of rice did. the Gita says it too: a leaf, a flower, offered with love, is accepted.

practice: Take one small thing, a flower, a sweet, a glass of water, and set it in front of a picture of Ganesha, or anywhere quiet. Offer it slowly, as to a guest you love. If you pray, say Om Gam Ganapataye Namah once.
If you don't, offer it in thanks to someone who has fed you.

wordCard.voice: Ganesh Chaturthi. Ganesha's fourth day: a clay guest welcomed home, offered what the family has with love, and given back to the water.

orig.note: Sanskrit gaṇeśa (lord of the ganas, his companions) + caturthī (the fourth lunar day).

carryVoice: Your line: God accepts what's offered with love. A handful of rice was enough. Until tomorrow.
